account: RL-Zero-Math changes the base by 0.24 % of its weight norm, and what carries the effect is a paired low-rank part: the top 8 singular input-output pairs per matrix (about 12 % of the change's squared norm), added to the base at 1.5x, match RL on new samples (hard328 200.25 vs 200.0 of 328 per sample, vote 216.25 vs 215.92, 0.88 of RL's per-sample lead on problems the cued base never solves in 4), while random, shifted-pair, one-sided or Think-SFT edits of the same norm do nothing.

Within that part, directions 2-8 (mostly early layers) switch the model into step-by-step deliberation and make each step less likely to slip, so they add right answers where the base finishes wrong (+13.5 points over a second base sample) or never succeeds; direction 1 and the late layers mostly make answers finish (removing the 8 directions doubles cap hits).

On-policy RL packs its change into such pairs whatever the reward (top-8 share 0.127 for LM-judge General-RL, 0.135 for Math, 0.030 for Think-SFT), on input directions that the base's step-by-step text already drives, so other fine-tunes share these subspaces (Think-SFT 4.8x chance, Code-RL 5.2x Think-SFT); only a reward's own input-output pairing carries its effect, and that effect stays in its domain (Code's pairs raise code pass rate by +7.0 points, Math's by +1.5).

Inference supplies the switch but not the lower slip rate: a three-token 'Okay' cue or a self-opened draw takes the plain base from 224 to 410-411 of 500, level with RL step 100 (418, where the cue still adds 1.7 points because not every step-100 sample opens that way), and T 1.0 instead of 0.6 stops long answers from looping (loop share past 4,096 tokens 0.004 vs 0.52-0.63).

Votes stand in for the lower slip rate only on problems the base already solves sometimes, because its wrong answers there scatter (same-problem agreement 0.26; real vs merged wrong answers +0.07 to +0.11 per vote), while a doubled cap or a forced commit finishes its cut answers without making them right.

So the untrained base reaches about 78 % of RL's one-sample gain on MATH-500 (410 on the 224-to-463 range), 68 % on hard328 (164 on 75-to-206) and 53-58 % on code, and under a vote of 4 RL stays 8.8 points ahead on hard328 because the base has no right sample on 26 of the 36 problems RL's vote wins.

consequences.claim: On hard328 the 1.5x top-8 edit is RL's own low-rank change (S1), so its per-problem right rate follows RL's problem by problem up to sample noise. Think-SFT has the same per-sample accuracy (0.651 vs 0.642 for the edit and 0.640 for RL) but none of RL's pairs and its own long-answer routes, so it tracks RL less. The correlation with RL is therefore higher for the edit than for Think-SFT by 0.01-0.26.
consequences.why_new: No fact or board result correlates per-problem right rates across models on hard328. F57/F58/F55 compare totals or a selected subset, where accuracy alone also explains them (F61 not separated). F65 compares wrong answers only, and result-bf6124 compares Think-SFT's difficulty profile on MATH-500 by profile rule, not against the edit.
consequences.statistic: D1 = Pearson r(edit rate, RL rate) - Pearson r(Think-SFT rate, RL rate) across hard328 problems; each rate is the right fraction of 4 samples (correlation difference, unitless)
consequences.rows: attempt 0 rows, samples 0-3 of each cell (restart rows attempt>0 dropped), problems present in all three cells; n counts problems (4 rows per problem per cell)
consequences.computation: 1) For each problem p and cell X, rate_X(p) = mean score_v3 over the 4 attempt-0 samples. 2) r_ER = Pearson correlation over problems of rate_edit and rate_RL; r_TR = same for rate_ThinkSFT and rate_RL. 3) D1 = r_ER - r_TR. 4) 90 % interval: 2000 bootstrap resamples of the problem ids with replacement (all of a problem's rows move together), recompute D1, take the 5th and 95th percentiles.
consequences.null: Difficulty alone (one latent axis): each model's 4-sample rate is a noisy reading of the same problem difficulty, so r(X,RL) = sqrt(rel_X * rel_RL) with rel from each model's own split-half resample (samples 0-1 vs 2-3, Spearman-Brown). Think-SFT is an accuracy-matched other model. Explore value of this null: D1 = 0.003.

consequences.claim: The same identity on MATH-500 (S1): one sample of the 1.5x top-8 edit with the cue (accuracy 0.940) follows RL's 4-sample per-problem rate more closely than one sample of Think-SFT with the cue does (accuracy 0.920-0.940, averaged over its 4 single samples). Matched accuracy and one sample on each side give equal noise, so only a shared mechanism can lift the edit's correlation; the account puts the gap at 0.02-0.54.
consequences.why_new: No fact correlates per-problem outcomes of the edit with RL on MATH-500. result-95a4dc reports only the edit's total (456 vs 457), result-5da8a9 pools 36 arms for union excess without singling out the edit, and result-bf6124 concerns Think-SFT's profile rule, not its agreement with RL against the edit's.
consequences.statistic: D2 = Pearson r(edit single-sample right, RL 4-sample rate) - mean over s=0..3 of Pearson r(Think-SFT sample s right, RL 4-sample rate), across MATH-500 problems (correlation difference, unitless)
consequences.rows: edit: its one row per problem; RL: attempt 0 samples 0-3; Think-SFT: attempt 0 samples 0-3 used one sample at a time; problems present in all three; n counts problems
consequences.computation: 1) rate_RL(p) = mean score_v3 of RL attempt-0 samples 0-3. 2) e(p) = edit score_v3 (0/1). 3) t_s(p) = Think-SFT sample s score_v3 for s = 0..3. 4) D2 = corr(e, rate_RL) - (1/4) * sum_s corr(t_s, rate_RL), Pearson over problems. 5) 90 % interval: 2000 bootstrap resamples of problem ids, recompute D2, 5th and 95th percentiles.
consequences.null: Accuracy alone: a single sample's correlation with RL's rate depends only on that sample's accuracy. Fit the line corr ~ accuracy over the 8 single non-edit samples (cued base samples 0-3 of rlneurons/day1_3/math500_base_cue-01 and Think-SFT samples 0-3), predict it at the edit's accuracy, and subtract Think-SFT's mean. Explore value 0.007.

consequences.claim: S3: a reward's own pairs carry its effect in its own domain. On HumanEval+/MBPP+, Code-RL's top-8 pairs at 1.5x should give per-problem pass outcomes that follow RL-Code's 3-seed pass rate, while RL-Math's top-8 pairs at 1.5x on the same problems, a near-random edit for code, should follow it only as much as their accuracy implies. The correlation gap is put at 0.065-0.49, above the accuracy-alone value of about 0.06.
consequences.why_new: F36/F37/F40 and result-a1bf75 report pass totals and whether fixes fall in the base's solved set. No fact or result correlates per-problem outcomes of the Code and Math edits with RL-Code's.
consequences.statistic: D3 = Pearson r(Code top-8 1.5x pass, RL-Code 3-seed pass rate) - Pearson r(Math top-8 1.5x pass, RL-Code 3-seed pass rate), across code problems (correlation difference, unitless)
consequences.rows: one row per problem (uid) in each cell; passed as 0/1; problems present in all five cells; n counts problems
consequences.computation: 1) rate_RC(p) = mean of passed over the three RL-Code cells (code1, hosts_s52, hosts_s53). 2) c(p) = passed in code_top8x1.5_code31; m(p) = passed in code_top8x1.5_math31. 3) D3 = corr(c, rate_RC) - corr(m, rate_RC), Pearson over problems. 4) 90 % interval: 2000 bootstrap resamples of problem uids, recompute D3, 5th and 95th percentiles.
consequences.null: Accuracy alone: a single-sample cell's correlation with RL-Code's rate is a linear function of its pass rate. Fit it over the non-Code-edit single cells (base_plain, base_cue, base_mathcue, the random rank-8 1.5x edit, the Math 1.5x edit), predict it at the Code edit's pass rate, and subtract the Math edit's correlation. Explore value 0.057.
